title: Curriculum concepts | Whole part
author: Nick Hart
summary: Nick Hart proposes 'whole part' as an anchoring concept for the infant years, arguing that it is useful well beyond maths and should shape teaching across the Foundation stage and KS1 curriculum. In maths he pairs 5 and 10 frames with the language of number bonds and gesture, and in English he connects phonics segmenting and blending to the part-whole structure of words. His most developed example is the sentence: focusing only on capital letters and full stops, he argues, leaves the least advantaged children without an understanding of what goes between them, so sentences should be taught as a naming part and an action part that later become noun and verb phrases. He then extends the model to nested places in geography, seasons and classification of living things in science, the dimensions of music and relationships in PSHE. The implication he draws is that a consistent representation such as a bar model should be a classroom staple, because explanations are transient and representations make the concept concrete and permanent.
points: Hart treats whole-part as a cross-curricular anchoring concept that children strengthen by meeting many examples across subjects, not just in maths.
He argues that defining a sentence by capital letters and full stops disadvantages children from less literature-rich homes, and that the naming and action parts must be specified explicitly.
The sentence model is given a progression: naming and action parts in the early years, then noun and verb phrases, adverbial phrases, and subject in KS2.
Geography's nested places and science's classification of living things are presented as part-whole structures that build early understanding of scale and classification.
He recommends a consistent representation such as the bar model across subjects because words and explanations are transient.
quotes: The whole part concept is fundamental to children’s learning in Foundation stage and KS1. It has such value that it is not just in maths where it is useful, but across a number of subjects.

There is of course the concrete counters on a 5 and 10 frame that is so important from the outset in Reception and continuing into KS1. But it is the language development that goes with this that makes it even more so: 1 and 4 make 5, 2 and 3 make 5 etc.
One of the most important concepts that children learn aged 4-7 is the sentence. How we talk about this with children can have significant ramifications as they move through the years.

If we focus attention on the presence of capital letters and full stops, it is quite conceivable that the least advantaged (who may have less access to a literature rich environment) do not learn the make up of what goes between those punctuation marks. There are some children who go all through primary still writing fragments or run on sentences.
The sentence is the whole; one complete thought. But this is not enough for some children. Specifying the parts is vital.
Whole part can be a useful anchoring concept for children that can be strengthened through knowing lots of examples from across the curriculum. It should therefore influence how we teach.
